utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone. Very briefly, Your Honours, in relation to what we discussed yesterday concerning Witness P019, let me just inform you that yesterday in the evening I succeeded in establishing telephone contact with him and he agreed to meet with me. Thus, I will attempt to be in Zagreb on Saturday and talk to him there, trying to convince him to come and testify next week. At any rate, I will inform the Court about the success of my endeavour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. You will by now, I'm sure, have seen the Court's order to try and support you further, as we said we would do, and that required his attendance next Wednesday. Mr. Vasic, are you ready for you next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning. -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Very briefly as the witness is coming in. With the Court's permission, may Mr. Theunens, the Prosecution's military expert, sit with us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see no objection. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for the witness, I hope that the interpreters can hear me well with the microphone even though I have the lectern in the way.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have your answer, Mr. Vasic, just as long as you keep your voice up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation which is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that the witness may have opened up papers. I don't have a clear view from here because of the screens. Could you deal with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lesanovic, you came to testify here. Please tell us what kind of papers you have in front of you, since we are interested here in your recollections and not in your notes. If you do have some notes, please explain what they are.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing special in my papers. As I was preparing for my evidence here, I noted down some things for myself, some talking points. It's of no relevance whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to put those papers aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, has this been clarified enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Let us begin. Please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Milovan Lesanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, since you and I speak the same language and since everything we say here in the courtroom has to be interpreted so that other persons present in the courtroom can understand what we're saying, I would like to ask you to make a short break after each question before proceeding with your answer. I would advise you to follow the cursor that you see on the screen. When you see that the sentence is completed, then you can begin with your answer. Also, I'd like to ask you to speak slowly because what you say needs to be interpreted, especially when mentioning names or units and things like that. Thank you. Please tell me, are you working or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of June of last year, I finished with my active military service and I am a colonel in retirement. In the meantime, I completed specialised studies, that is to say before I retired I did so, at the Department of Civilian Defence. I completed studies in security management which deals with security of persons and property. Now I'm employed as a security manager in a private company.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell me what kind of schools you completed within your military career and what kind of jobs you performed while you were an officer before you retired.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the Military Academy for Anti-Aircraft Defence in Zadar in 1973. Following that, I was assigned to work in Sabac where I spent three years as platoon commander. Following that, I was for ten years battery commander serving in Belgrade. And then for three years I was commander of an artillery battalion in Pozarac, following that three years commander of anti-aircraft defence in the Guards Brigade, three years commander of rocket and artillery units within the special units. Then for three years I was commander of the 1st Rocket Brigade of Anti-Aircraft Defence. That was the post that I held in 1999 during the aggression. Following that, I served as chief of artillery rocket units of anti-aircraft defence in the 1st Army, and then the last three years before I retired I was deputy and chief of defence of the Republic of Serbia in the Ministry of Defence of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lesanovic. Please tell me, when did you come to the Guards Brigade. You told us that at some point in time you served within that unit.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I came to the Guards Brigade in 1989 after completing command staff school for air force and anti-aircraft defence. I was assigned chief of rocket and artillery units of anti-aircraft defence with the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade. I spent three years in that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If my math is correct, you were in that post in 1991, which is the period of time that we're interested in, when the Guards Motorised Brigade was tasked with participating in the operations at the front in Vukovar and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, do you know when the Guards Motorised Brigade came to the Vukovar sector, where it was billeted, and where its headquarters were?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The Motorised Guards Brigade came there pursuant to the order of the chief of General Staff since at that time it was associated with the cabinet of the chief of General Staff. Pursuant to the order of the commander on the 13th [as interpreted] of September, 1991, at 1500 hours it was sent on march in that area. They arrived at around that time in the Negoslavci sector where the headquarters was established. The units were deployed in that area in accordance with the task given to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lesanovic. I have a comment concerning the transcript. Instead of 13th September it should be 30th of September. Mr. Lesanovic, you said that it was pursuant to the order of the chief of the General Staff. We heard here from some witnesses that the Guards Brigade actually was subordinated to the cabinet of the federal secretary of defence. Is that what you have in mind or you still think it was subordinated to the chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a slip of tongue. It was subordinated to the chef de cabinet or Chief of Staff of the federal defence secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that you came to Negoslavci, that headquarters was established there. You were chief of air force and anti-aircraft defence within the Guards Motorised Brigade. Please tell me, who was your immediate superior and then who was above him and how did the command of the Guards Brigade function.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The duty of the chief of artillery and rocket units -- rather, that chief, just like all other chiefs, have their own specialty. And my first, immediate superior was Colonel Aric Chief of Staff. My second superior was colonel, and then later on General Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about how the headquarters functioned. Can you tell us how orders were issued. Who took part in preparing the orders and commands?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I will be brief. Let me give you an example that, of an assignment that we were given. As soon as the guards brigade was given its tasks, the commander with the inner circle, since there's -- there was sufficient time to carry out that assignment, that task, and to prepare it, the commander could implement a regular procedure for issuing an order together with his immediate associates, the inner circle. They studied the task assigned to us. They prepared a plan for draft order. It was done by the command. After this plan, this proposal was advanced by various assistants and specialist chiefs, a proposal was made to the commander of the Guards Brigade. The commander decides whether he wants to adopt it or not. In this case, the commander adopted this without any hesitation, and that was the first decision to go on a march from Belgrade, from the Marsal Tito Barracks to Vukovar -- or that is to say to Negoslavci. This is the principle that on the basis of which decisions were made. However, if for some reason it needed to be done urgently, then an abbreviated method was used. Certain preparations were dropped in order to gain time. Based on that, one can see that the work of the command of the Guards Brigade was very efficient and well-organised. People worked jointly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, this abbreviated procedure, was it also a product of collective work or was it done only by individuals?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the case of an abbreviated procedure, all organs participate, too, but given that there isn't sufficient time, certain steps are shortened in order to comply with the time. Only what is important is stated. This abbreviated procedure can be used in combat as well, as necessary. There is no need to repeat something that's already been decided upon and implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the march, the arrival in Negoslavci. Tell me, please, who was your -- or rather, who was your unit subordinated to upon your arrival in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade -- or rather, when we arrived in Negoslavci, there was already the command of the Operations Group South there. Colonel Bojat Bajo headed it. I don't know what the reasons for that were. This lasted for several days. I couldn't really give you the exact dates now, but after some time, most likely due to the fact that they were inefficient in their command, Colonel Bajo Bojat was moved to another post. He had to withdraw from that area, and the command of the Guards Brigade headed by Colonel Mrksic, pursuant to the order of the commander of the 1st Army, and there was an earlier order resubordinating the Guards Brigade to the 1st Military District. So pursuant to the order of the commander of the 1st Military District, commander of the Guards Brigade, and the entire brigade took over the role that had previously been assigned to the Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say the command of the Guards Brigade took over the functions previously performed by the Operations Group South. Was that in accordance with the rules and the military doctrine that were in force at the time, for them to take over the role of the command of the operations group in this manner?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that it was a good thing for the unit that was supposed to implement this task. First of all, it wasn't good for the commander and it wasn't good for the Guards Brigade since we had sufficient obligations as it was, obligations pertaining to our own brigade. In addition to the Guards Brigade, we were now assigned additional tasks that we were supposed to carry out in parallel. So the normal procedure would have been to have the command of the 1st Military District issue an order where they would specify the complement, what complement that would be, so that independently of the Guards Brigade there should have been a command, a miniature perhaps, but still a command, a separate command, of the Operations Group South, whose task would have been to coordinate the units and their tasks in that area. As it was, the command of the Guards Brigade in addition to all of its existing tasks had to also carry out those that were assigned to the Operations Group South. We had many logistics problems, problems with security in the rear because this command, which was not expanded at all, especially the section dealing with logistics issues, had to also take care of supplies, supplies of ammunition, and everything else. So you can imagine what a huge job it was for everyone, what huge efforts had to be invested into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. One thing I'd like to ask you is to keep the same pace as before. I think this answer was particularly speedy. You should just stick to your previous pace. What sort of a unit is an operations group? Is that larger or smaller than a brigade? What is the purpose of setting up an operations group and how long does it usually last before it's outlived its useful life, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Operations Group South specifically was set up in order to unify all the available forces in the area around Vukovar, where the operations were under way. Since there were many different units with different affiliations, it was necessary and in keeping with the regulations then as now to place all activities, especially combat activities in a given area, under a single command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is it the established practice to have these units set up at the brigade level or at the corps level?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you look at this particular example, there were two or three brigades in that area; and operations groups are established wherever there are more units than a single brigade. At the time there were corps commands; however, an operations group is a temporary unit, a provisional unit, set up whenever needed and wherever needed in order to unify all these different units. It's somewhat more than a brigade you might say but somewhat less than a corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would I be wrong in suggesting that it is the corps command that exercises command over a unit that is composed of various brigades?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the situation that prevailed in Vukovar and the need to exercise command over several brigade in one and the same area, would the role of the operations group not be something that would be more equivalent to the structure of a corps rather than that of a -- of an ordinary brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the number and size of units in the area, the corps commands had nothing less, especially under the circumstances at the time. This job, to unify all the provisional forces in the area, was a much more difficult one than simply commanding a corps. Within a corps you have the normal peacetime organisation, you know the people, everything functions; whereas here you have different bodies, different units, that you first have to familiarise yourself with in just one area, regardless of whether you found them there or brought them in yourself. You need to have these units organised, linked-up, and you need to use them to carry out your assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This promotion of the command of the Guards Brigade to a command supposed to control and command much larger units in terms of their organisation, did that affect the work of these commands and did that make their work more difficult throughout their time in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The work was certainly made more difficult because of this. Again, the Guards Brigade command in addition to it's own more than sufficient commitments with their own unit at the same time had to carry out all these other tasks that we have referred to. I don't think it's too difficult to imagine what an effort that must have been, what an overstretch. Quite unacceptable for the circumstances. But, to put it quite simply, it didn't affect any developments or any measures that were taken in a bad way because measures were taken to protect the population, to protect the men, to protect the equipment, and to carry out any assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did Operations Group South last for as long as you were in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of November, the command of Operations Group South was functioning. That same day, pursuant to an order of the command of the 1st Military District, the entire command archive, all the files, the so-called secret command TKT was handed over to the 80th Motorised Brigade from Kragujevac. After that on the 23rd, the command of the Guards Brigade, once preparations had been carried out, on the 24th conducted a march between Vukovar and Belgrade to bring the unit back to its garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please have Exhibit 425 on our monitors. This is a regular combat report of the Operations Group South command in relation to the 22nd of November, 1991. This is precisely what the witness has been speaking about. If we could please zoom in slightly on the other half of this document. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, would you please be so kind and slowly read from this document to us the last two passages of item 2, not item 3, item 2.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean, "In the course of..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: "In the course of the 22nd of November, 1991, pursuant to your order strictly confidential number 115151" --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lesanovic, I didn't say four passages, I said the last two. The last two passages of item 2. It says: "In the course of the day ..."

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just take it easy, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: "In the course of the day, all measures were taken for the 80th Motorised Brigade to take over all the functions in terms of organisation and command in the area of responsibility of OG South. The command of the 80th Motorised Brigade has received all the instructions and documents to organise control and command in the area of responsibility of OG South."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Lesanovic, are these paragraphs not in relation to the issue concerning the handover of documents, of files, which is what you spoke about a while ago?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall no longer be requiring this exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would now like to go back to your specific role in the arrival of that Guards Motorised Brigade in the Negoslavci area. You told you were chief of artillery and rocket units of the anti-aircraft defence at the time. Can you please tell us how your own branch was organised in the Vukovar theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Everything was very much geared to the assignments we had received pursuant to a decision by the commander of the Guards Brigade, plus the light self-propelled artillery and rocket division of the anti-aircraft defence, which received the assignment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an order to start a march for the PVO, the anti-aircraft defence, and this was part of a formation order of the Guards Brigade command to execute that march.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you for a second, please. You were talking about the light self-propelled artillery battalion, but we don't know which other unit that unit was part of.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was part of the Guards Brigade. I'm talking about the Guards Brigade and how it arrived in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please proceed. I'm sorry for the interruption, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that the artillery battalion had been mobilised, it had within its composition a command, a command battery, two self-propelled artillery batteries, 20/3 BOV 3, a rocket battery known as Strela 1M, and a logistics platoon or a rear platoon. As all the other units, the artillery battalion, too, received an assignment to carry out a march within a single column and also in terms of its anti-aircraft defence responsibilities. Having arrived at the destination of the march, the anti-aircraft defence artillery battery, based on a pre-established plan, was deployed in a certain area where its deployment area was, deployment sector was determined or defined, its assignment was defined. Air reconnaissance and reporting was organised, a system was established, and a command post was determined. These assignments were carried out by the artillery battalion in the area, the objective being to protect all the units based on a pre-established plan and for anti-aircraft defence purposes. If I remember correctly - I should go back to my documents to check this because I'm not certain - the artillery battalion had to complete this assignment by the 12th or the 13th without any special link-up with the anti-aircraft defence system itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you for a minute. You said by the 12th or the 13th. Which month, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: October. I'm sorry, October.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: On this day we received an assignment to link-up with the anti-aircraft defence system of the 12th Corps. I assume that the corps command had received this assignment from their superior command, the command of the 1st Military District. The assignment was to unify all the available forces in the area and to organise for the link-ups.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me whether you as a unit had been resubordinated to the corps by this time or --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The brigade -- or rather, the artillery battalion had not been resubordinated. It was still part of the Guards Brigade in terms of organisation and structure. It was the Guards Brigade that carried out assignments as part of OG South, which is the unit that I spoke of before. All this lasted until the 8th of November when the Guards Brigade took over -- or rather, there had been an order by the command of the 1st Military District, making the Guards Brigade at the same time the command of OG South, putting them in charge of OG South. So on the 9th - I'll try to avoid repeating what I've spoken about already - an assignment was received, a decision was made, and in keeping with this decision, as this was about anti-aircraft defence, an order was written - I drafted the order myself in relation to the anti-aircraft defence - defining the tasks of all anti-aircraft [Realtime transcript read in error "anti-tank"] defence forces in the area. The PVO anti-aircraft defence order as well as all other orders pertaining to all the other branches are part of the formation of the commander of OG South. You have a map on which you produce an anti-aircraft defence plan, and this is something that the chief of the anti-aircraft defence must produce.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. One correction. Page 15, line 15, this is about the task for all anti-aircraft defence forces in the area, and here we see "anti-tank." I think there is an error there.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: If I may just complete my question -- my answer. Certain tasks were envisaged for the light self-propelled artillery battalion of the Guards Brigade according to deployment sectors and specific tasks. The light self-propelled rocket and artillery battalion of the 80th Motorised Brigade and the batteries of the 211th Armoured Brigade -- or rather, its artillery battalion. A PVO order is forwarded to all units and it is available to everyone. The order was submitted to all the organisational units of the Guards Brigade and the remaining units within OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you say this, does that mean that, for example, infantry units within a certain other unit also had PVO tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: PVO is for all units.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, PVO is short for anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For all the units that have within their composition anti-aircraft defence units, and we did. We had light artillery platoons, we had rocket detachments, rocket squads. In addition to PVO tasks, protecting the air space, the tasks of the other units with no PVO forces was to organise a system of protection and to take steps to ensure that the men were protected from air attacks as well as equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This order that you wrote, did it effectively resubordinate the units of the light artillery battalion of the PVO of the 80th Brigade and the light artillery battalion of the 211th Brigade? Did this order resubordinate these units to the Guards Brigade, rather OG South or did they remain within the composition of their own units?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The PVO artillery battery of the 80th Motorised Brigade remained throughout an organisational unit belonging to the 80th Brigade, which means there was no resubordination. It was just added to the PVO system in order to have better deployment in the area, in order to organise combat, and in order to ensure timely receipt of information on anything that was moving through the air space, if anything, and in order to be able to take timely measures and act. The PVO artillery battalion at the outset, which is what I was talking about, was part of the PVO system of the 12th Corps, but it had never been resubordinated. It was only in the sense of its specialty or in a specialised sense that it was part of this other unit. Much along the same lines, this artillery battalion was linked-up in terms of purely specialised tasks, but it wasn't formally resubordinated. The command of the 80th Brigade remained in the command of this particular artillery battalion belonging to the 80 Brigade and everything went through the artillery battalion command except for these other things that were linked up and in keeping with the command when and under what circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just one correction on page 17, lines 4 and 5, when you were talking about the needs -- the need to have these units linked-up with the PVO system, you were talking about -- you were talking about an order to go into combat and the transcript says in order to organise combat. So please, when you use abbreviations, tell us what that means. What is "VOJ," the word that you used?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: That is short for air surveillance reporting and -- air surveillance and reporting, being one element of the PVO. PVB is anti-aircraft combat and PVZ is anti-aircraft protection. All three of these elements of the PVO are essential and they must be linked-up. It is for this reason that PVO units or artillery and rocket units of the PVO must be linked-up within this system and be unified. What is air surveillance and reporting? The elements of the VOJ are the centres of air surveillance and reporting which exist at the artillery battalion level, battalion level, and at higher level headquarters, but not at battalion level. The task of the centre is to organise all information, to receive information from all possible sources. What must be organised is also which centres are listened to, at what frequency for a certain area. One listens to one's own sources, which is a radar surveillance stations, visual surveillance stations. This is then put on a plotting grid, and all this information at a certain frequency is conveyed to all structures and bodies that have the right equipment to receive this information. At lower levels, at battery levels, there are just the plotting grids; these are usually in code. Under a VOJ code there is a quadrant, and in relation to that that the situation in the air is monitored. Let me just say something else. This plotting grid is normally 60 by 60. It's kept at a battery command post. There are concentric circles there, 20, 40, and 60 kilometres. These are lines of readiness which are determined in keeping with the training level of the units. If the unit is well trained, then they don't have to put in greater effort in terms of establishing their readiness. It doesn't need to be 40 or 60 kilometres, 20 kilometres is sufficient. And if the unit is not well trained, then proportionately the readiness line is moved. Once this information is received, commanders of batteries proceed to implement it, that is to say they fire at enemy targets within the air space.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained this in great detail. Please tell us what was your role as PVO chief in this system of anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: As I have explained to you at the outset, since I was a specialised organ of the Chief of Staff, in this case I was the chief of air force and anti-aircraft defence and in addition to preparing these mandatory documents I also had to monitor and coordinate the work of all units in the entire area and provide any specialised advice as needed. It was also my task to propose certain measures to the commander of OG South in order to move, relocate certain forces in order to ensure efficient support to our forces on the ground and to ensure better organisation of anti-aircraft defence or PVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say to move certain forces or formations. Please tell us, who is in command of light artillery battalion formations of the 80th and 211th Brigade at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The 211th brigade -- or rather, the battery from the artillery battalion of the 211th Brigade was resubordinated, and since it was deployed with a special task it was under the command of the battery commander. As for the artillery battalion of anti-aircraft defence of the 80th Brigade, the commander of the artillery battalion was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander resubordinated to, the commander of the artillery battalion of the 80th Brigade -- or rather, who was the superior?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The superior was the commander of the 80th Brigade. So the commander of the artillery battalion, that unit was constantly under the 80th Brigade and it was linked-up with the anti-aircraft defence structure when it came to these particular specialist tasks. This was all a matter of internal organisation. Commander of the artillery battalion of anti-aircraft defence sent regular reports to the command of the 80th Brigade, which in turn sent all reports jointly to the command of OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you say "jointly," what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: It means that the commander of the 80th Brigade received reports from all commanders of battalions, artillery battalions that were under his command. And then after compiling all of these reports, including the anti-aircraft defence artillery battalions, they would compile it all together and then forward it to OG South in writing on a daily basis. These were regular reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Under whose command would this unit LAD PVO of the 80th Brigade be able to change its firing position or its command post?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the PVO artillery battalion? Well, if necessary, it could be done under -- pursuant to the orders of the commander of the 80th Brigade. They could move that unit or relocate it. However, commander of the artillery battalion is responsible within his area of responsibility, and it was his duty to inform me as chief of anti-aircraft defence. It was his duty to inform me about this because I was in charge of keeping accurate records and entering all the information on the working plan, because deployment of all units had to be reflected accurately in the working plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will go back to this issue later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But could we now see Exhibit 367, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Which is precisely the order concerning anti-aircraft defence which you spoke about and I would like to cover certain items with you in this order because you said that you drafted this order. Mr. Lesanovic, can you see this order on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is this the order for PVO that you drafted? And if so, who was it forwarded to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: This order is the one that I drafted pursuant to the order of the commander of OG South. I was duty-bound to do that as commander of PVO. It was forwarded to all organisational units which comprised OG South, starting assault attachments, 1, 2, 3, 4, and then proceeding to all other units which had PVO units, but also to those which did not have PVO units within their composition for the reasons I stated earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the heading of this order. It says here: "To the command of the 80th LAD PVO." Can you explain what this means?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: This means that this order relates to the 80th Motorised Brigade. Since they were a part of that unit as a specialised force, this is how one formulates it in an order. This is why it says here: "To the 80th LAD." And then the similar thing is done within the command -- signal corps and -- signals corps and other specialised sections, so that the command upon receiving this can then disseminate it to appropriate units. Before making their own decisions, they're duty-bound to study it carefully, to analyse what task was issued to them, and then in a brief decision-making process they have to propose to their commander how their respective units are to be used. So this is a developed pattern on how such orders are implemented. This was done at the level of OG South as well, using a similar methodology and then the same is done at lower levels, particularly in this case we are analysing the 80th Brigade. And this is why it is addressed to the artillery battalion, not because the artillery battalion was resubordinated, not because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did other organisational units receive similar copies of this order, other units within OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this particular copy has relevant information on the last page. I myself have a copy where it is specified precisely who received this order. And all of these people had to confirm the receipt by their signature. I don't know if you have it on your copy, but if not we can look at my copy, which is identical to this one. That is to say that assault detachments, 1, 2, 3, 4, received an identical order addressed in the same way, but that is not to say that all of these units were resubordinated to the PVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. It's all clear to me now. Can you tell us, please, in the right corner of this order it says: "Copy number 2." What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: What I said to you earlier, it says here: "Handover for command purposes," so that's what I explained to you already. And then it says here: "Copy number 2," that is to say this is copy number 2 and copy number 1 remains with OG South. Copy number 2 is the one that's disseminated. What's missing here, most likely it was not recorded, is enclosure number. When one types a cover letter that goes with an order, then normally it is recorded as enclosure number, I don't know, 1, 2, 10, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that in the upper right corner it says: "Handover together with the order." Can you explain this in greater detail, please. What was the procedure involved?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Together with an order of the commander of OG South - I don't need to repeat this to you again, that this defines all steps linked with the implementation of the tasks, specifying tasks for each particular unit and all other related matters. So this particular order is an integral part of the original order, and it is enclosed with this original order. This is why it says here: Enclosure number such and such. So based on existing records, they would prepare a cover letter that would accompany this, and then they would specify what enclosure number this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please tell me that there -- you said that there was an order of the commander of OG South. Who was it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: That order was sent to the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, if this is the example that you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us analyse this order. Would you please look at item 1 of this item. It pertains to an attack that is to be carried -- rather, that was carried out by the enemy, the Croatian side. It was an air attack. Can you tell us what activities the Croatian side undertook from -- with their aircraft, whether any bombs were dropped, what detonation they produced, and what else you can tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the first item, as far as PVO is concerned, they need to provide basic information about the enemy - in this case, this was the Ustasha forces - and their resources and capabilities in the area of air force. They didn't have any lethal weaponry, but here we have an information as to what they had available. It is certain that they supplied their units and they also conducted evacuations. What they did is that since they knew what our resources were, is that they would fly at the level of 2.000 metres or 3.000 metres. They would do it in an unplanned way, and since they didn't have proper ammunition they would drop from the air water boilers that were filled with certain items and that would spread panic and cause certain losses and would affect the morale of our forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did they also fly over in helicopters? I can see here that they are mentioning a Bell make helicopter. Can you explain what type of a helicopter this is.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the information that we received, as I told you after all of the reports were compiled by the 12th Corps, we detected that they attempted to fly over. They were detected by our radars and also by units of the 12th Corps in that area. They attempted to fly over in two helicopters. After fire was opened, they did not reach the area of other units because the units of the Guards Brigade opened fire. We have no information as to what happened to them. One helicopter aborted its mission, gave up and went back, and following that we had no helicopter flights over our area. There were two UTVA flights, and they dropped the boilers, the ones that I described to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I assume you're speaking of assault flights. Tell us, please, do you know about the Croatian helicopter landing at the Sloga stadium for some transportation purposes?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, most likely, because they transported those who were wounded and sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know when they did this? Do you know anything about the period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say, but it was recorded and it was recorded in various log-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please look at the second paragraph of item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It says: "In the activities so far, except for H/P, the Ustasha units were not active against the forces of OG South." What does this mean.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to those two initial helicopter flights, there were no additional activities of the enemy; however, the PVO units had to be on full alert because one never knows. It was possible that they would attempt to surprise us, which would adversely affect our morale and cause us to suffer some losses. So our mission was to prevent them from opening fire from the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now, would you please read for yourself item 2 of this order and would you please explain it to us.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the first item you saw basic information about the aircraft of the enemy in the air space, and then the second item speaks of the tasks that were assigned to units. This is a typical procedure. There, in this item, the task for all units is defined, also the deployment of units is defined, and it is specified how they are to open fire. This applied to the artillery battalion of the Guards Brigade, artillery battalion of the 80th Brigade, and that of the 211th Brigade. That is to say that this item specifies only the tasks assigned to the PVO units, especially the task they had in order to link-up, in order to organise, in order to avoid a situation where after being deployed in this area there would be certain dead corners that would not be covered by our forces. And potentially that was dangerous because the enemy aircraft could fly over those areas undetected. And that was the purpose of this attempt to unify everything. The -- item 2 specifies how to take an organised command post, and I was involved in this personally. All tasks were explained in detail, and any remaining clarifications were to be given on the ground. Needless to say, this item also determines the place where the commanders of these subordinate units are supposed to report for PVO and in order to receive this particular assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say the commanders of subordinate units for PVO. Can you please clarify that. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of air surveillance and reporting and anti-aircraft defence is not the commander. He has no powers to command any unit except in a unified PVO system. To have all PVO units linked-up in a unified system to coordinate their work and to provide assistance in terms of military specialty and to make it possible for those units to carry out their tasks in as easy a manner as possible, but that is not exercising direct command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: These here, which chain of command are they a part of? For example, the light artillery and rocket battalion of the PVO of the 80th Brigade, motorised brigade, who is it subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a constituent unit of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Purely in terms of PVO they received an assignment in this sector, in this area, with this assignment here, special positions and be at the ready to carry out this mission along this axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Given this assignment, does that not constitute effectively a resubordination of this unit and an extraction of this unit from the command chain of the 80th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, this is no resubordination at all. This is no taking it away from the chain of command of the 80th Brigade. The PVO artillery battalion is part and parcel of the brigade, and it is linked-up with the overall system only to carry out this special-purpose mission. The mission being to fire at any planes flying through the area, but they can't do this on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, would this be a convenient time for our first break, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. We will adjourn now and resume at ten minutes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, can we please proceed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the break we spoke about the order for PVO, which is Exhibit 367 in this trial. You explained some of the individual paragraphs and items of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we please have page 2 of the same order displayed on our monitors. I'm interested in item 7, that is the lower half of page 2. The number of this page is -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, you see that in this order the light self-propelled rocket and artillery battalion of the 80th Motorised Brigade was placed at the disposal of OG South until the 11th of November. From thereon it was sent to the rear security of the motorised brigade. Can you tell us why this was done in this case and what this means in practical terms.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The 80th Motorised Brigade came to the Vukovar area in stages. As the artillery battalion and a part of the brigade command were the first to arrive and were the first to join this mission, it was necessary to organise its logistics. It wasn't in itself equipped to look after its own supplies, and that was not part of the plan simply because it was much simpler to do what had been envisaged up until the 11th, for it to work on the logistics of the Guards Brigade. And then after that, once the logistics battalion of the 80th Motorised Brigade had arrived, from this moment on the brigade command was independent in terms of its logistics. Among other things, it committed to look after its own PVO artillery battalion in terms of any logistics support. That is the reason behind this sentence in the order. Regardless of the fact that the PVO artillery battalion had within its composition a logistics platoon, a logistics platoon, our decision was it would be simpler for them to get their own food supplies and whatever else rather than have another logistics platoon deployed at the rear, but this was not a lasting solution. One believed at the time that things could be dealt with by this date and that the brigade could deal with its own logistics without any outside assistance, I mean the 80th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We see this order was drafted on the 9th of November, and the OG South logistics commitment to this unit was only until the 11th of November; right? As far as OG South was concerned, that was only for two days; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please go to the last page of this order, this PVO order. I'm talking about item 10, the ERN number is 04699061. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, can you see item 10? It says: "Reports." Can you please look at item 10 and please comment on it. Tell us about this reporting between PVO units, how exactly did that work?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The reports can be regular ones or interim ones. Regular reports are what is envisaged here. These must be submitted to cover any activity undertaken by the rocket and artillery units and any potential action taken by the Ustasha air force, and this is attached to other regular reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you say "attached to regular reports," whose and to whom?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The regular reports of the unit period to the artillery battalion, that's the brigade command, which unifies under its command all the artillery battalions and then this report is submitted to the command of the OG South. From the command of the 80th Brigade there is just one report that reaches the OG South command post in Negoslavci. So, so much for regular reports. Of course there is always the commitment of the PVO chief, where there is one, and the commanders, such as regulated here that any change in the firing positions and command posts of these artillery battalions must immediately be reported. That is a duty. These reports must be received by 1800 hours with the situation as recorded at 1700 hours. When you have interim reports, when something exceptional happens, that is when something extraordinary happens and that something that has nothing to do with the subject matter of the normal, regular reports. There is no particular date or time set for these. These are sent in whenever a need arises to have these interim reports, indeed because something exceptional occurred or because there was something that was affecting the combat readiness. And then this is then sent in to a superior command so that they can take appropriate measures. My apologies. So this report, for example, is nothing special, as compared to the report defining the reporting system as to the basic order of the commander of OG South. That's harmonised, and the only reason this was produced is because this goes directly to the commander -- or rather, the PVO chief, the chief of the rocket and artillery units within organisational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: For example, within the 80th Motorised Brigade, who makes sure that unit reports such as this light PVO artillery and rocket battalion are sent to the OG South command?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Under the rules, the commander of the battalion is in charge of both regular reports and interim reports. He provides answers to all these questions on a daily basis and then submits these answers to the chief at the brigade level. The chief meets other chiefs and joins this up. He takes notice of whatever he thinks is important and then submits this information to the operative organ of the command of the 80th Brigade, who then unifies all this information and submits it to Operations Group South. Where there is nothing, where nothing was written, where nothing is defined or there is no PVO chief or the PVO chief failed to respond and after mobilisation had been carried out and he was the PVO chief because the PVO chief was from the reserve forces, in such cases this is directly submitted by a unit commander, and this unit commander can be in one of the units at this level or he can be a chief. When needed in the process of decision-making, he can then go back to his command post and the command of the artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said pursuant to this order the LAD PVO of the 80th Brigade was not resubordinated to Operations Group South, but rather remained as part of the 80th Brigade. Can you tell me about the period of time between the 9th of November when this order was written and the 21st of November, 1991. Based on what you know, did the LAD PVO artillery battalion ever get resubordinated or taken out of the composition of the 80th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there is no document to show that and there was never any need for them to leave their own original composition, their own brigade. Accordingly, there was no resubordination there. It was an organisational entity within its own brigade. As for its PVO tasks, it carried out the PVO tasks in this joint manner, but that applied to all the other PVO units, not just to this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit 368 displayed on our monitors. This is a regular combat report of the command of OG South, the 21st of November, 1991. Thank you very much. I'll try to keep that in mind. This is Exhibit 368, regular combat report of the OG South command. The date is the 21st of November, 1991. If we can please blow up the other part of this report where it says "OG South units."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, can you please have a look. Have a look at this regular combat report of the OG South command. Can you read through this portion here shown on the monitor and tell us if there's an order there to have the LAD PVO artillery battalion of the 80th Motorised Brigade returned to its original unit, having previously been resubordinated, if --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's assume that it was at one point resubordinated. In that case, there would have to be an order regulating that, and the OG South command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Does the Court have the document in English? Our system seems to have gone down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We seem to have it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lesanovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Just like in certain moments and in certain orders, the OG South command - and it probably exists in one of the documents - clearly defined which units were to be resubordinated. Likewise, the command defining this resubordination is duty-bound to issue an order to determine the exact time when a subordinated -- resubordinated unit is to leave and return to its own unit, to its original unit. But this doesn't transpire from the face of this document, and there's no document to indicate that, that the PVO artillery battalion was ever resubordinated to the Guards Brigade -- or rather, to the command of OG South because, I repeat, there was no need for anything like that to be done, there was no reason. Had this been necessary, I'm sure it would have been reflected in one of the documents. I don't see for what reason this PVO artillery battalion could possibly have been resubordinated to anyone, since it was deployed right here in the area of responsibility of its own brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lesanovic, in other words it does not transpire from this combat report that the artillery battalion of the 80th Brigade is in question and you as the chief of the PVO have told us that this artillery battalion was never sent out of its original unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object to that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on a very critical issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. Thank you, Your Honour. This only followed up on the series of answers given by the witness, but I will withdraw from eliciting this particular answer. Let's leave it with what the witness has already said in his previous answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, in keeping with the rules, did you at any point during your stay in the territory of Vukovar as the chief of the PVO, did you ever receive information that the LAD PVO of the 80th Motorised Brigade changed its command post? And if you were informed of that, pursuant to whose orders was this done?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Pursuant to the request, i.e., the order of the commander of the 80th Brigade, the commander of the artillery battalion of the PVO carried out the transfer of its command post from the previously assigned post to the Ovcara sector. Obviously, nothing substantial changed with that, and I suppose that the commander of the 80th Brigade knew exactly why he had done that. There must have been a plan underlying that move. There was nothing in dispute when it came to the fact that the command post was changed, and I believe that one battery was also moved on that occasion. But the system has -- did not suffer, and there was no need to correct that order by the commander of the 80th Brigade. The artillery battalion commander informed me about that to -- to help me follow the working map of the chief of the PVO who had to have reliable information at any given point in time on the deployment of the units in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, if one were to use this LA PD battalion were some action that does not involve the PVO, for some action on the ground, pursuant to whose orders this would have been done and whose orders would the commander of the LA PD follow in order to perform this task?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The capabilities of the artillery rocket units, and especially late artillery battalions, involves action on ground. And this action is number 2 in priorities; the number 1 priority is the anti-aircraft protection. So this second priority would be carried out pursuant to the order or the request of the brigade commander, on which strength it is deployed. In addition to protecting a certain area, the area of the air, it also supports the action on the ground of the units of the 80th Brigade. So this would be done pursuant to the order of the commander of the 80th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And if there was a need for the LA PD artillery battalion to be used in establishing the command of a certain place or establishing military authorities in a certain place, pursuant to whose orders could that unit be appointed the command of that place?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: All the other issues, the engagement of the commander of the artillery battalion within his area of responsibility are within the purview of his commander. In this case, this is the brigade commander. It is his entitlement to regulate the tasks of his subordinate units and commanders thereof. Amongst other things, the engagement on other issues that have nothing to do with the PVO, obviously bearing in mind that this does not have an influence on the primary task of the artillery battalion. In other words, if the brigade commander so estimates that the -- the artillery battalion commander can perform other tasks, those tasks will be given to that commander. Since there are several commanders, the brigade commander will issue an order according to his estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: During your stay in the Vukovar sector, did you have information whether the LA PD artillery battalion of the 80th Brigade was ever appointed to command a certain place?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The artillery battalion commander of the LA PD of the 80th Brigade after the change of the command post - I suppose this was part of the preparations for the task that had been given to him by the brigade commander - an order was issued to him to become commander of Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say that you were informed by --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The artillery battalion commander. I believe that there is a document to the effect that the brigade commander regulated that. I did not ask for that document because this was not relevant for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just tell me, commander of what brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The 80th Brigade. His own brigade, his superior commander, the commander of the 80th Brigade appointed him the place commander of Ovcara. And I believe that it was based on his estimate because the battalion commander at that time was an active officer, as opposed to all the others who were reserve officers. I believe that it was his estimate that that particular commander was best suited for that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, at the moment when you learned that, was this unit in the area of responsibility of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the area of responsibility of the 80th Motorised Brigade. That's -- that was the deployment, that there was to be a link-up and they were to be in the area of responsibility of their own brigade and that they -- at the same time they could provide support to the units of their own brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me something, please. Where was the central observation point during the operations in Vukovar, the artillery units of the PVO observation post, and where were you during those activities in the territory of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: My stay was predominantly in the sector of deployment of the PVO artillery battalion of the Guards Brigade; in other words, in the command post where the operations centre was -- or rather, operations centre of the Operations Group South. Pursuant to the order for anti-aircraft defence and since we did not have any other equipment, I said that this centre was of a temporary character, we made use of the available equipment of the Guards Brigade. And we placed them in the function of the activities of the OG South. This is where my post was supposed to be, and that was in the vicinity of the winery. Since that area is rather flat and the visibility is rather low, during the activities of surveillance it occurred to me that the area of the winery, which is the roof itself towards the very highest part of it, was enough for the surveillance of the entire area of Vukovar and its general area. In conditions of good visibility, one could see the entire area very well. It was the forward command post, to put it that way. The term is not good. It was not exactly a forward command post, but since that centre of the operations group, the surveillance post of the operations group could not be placed anywhere better, this place to me and other bodies of the artillery battalion command provided us with a possibility to be able to monitor and control the work of our units, all those who were engaged in those actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see Exhibit 156. It's a map of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And I will kindly ask you to point to that point that you have just described for us as the place where you were situated during the armed actions that took place in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we blow up the part around the barracks and Velepromet? I believe this is enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to provide the witness with a magic pen, and I am going to ask the witness to put a circle around the place where he was and put a number 1 next to that circle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the vicinity of Velepromet, across the road from it and below the barracks, that's number 1. Isn't that so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. And thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We won't need this map anymore. I would like to tender this map into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 773, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, tell me, please, the commanders of the PVO units, did they come to you, to this place that you just pointed to us, for daily briefings?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no need for them to come every day. If they did come, they would do it only occasionally, and one of those occasions was when I gave them their tasks. From that area, we had a good visibility of the entire region, and I would sometimes ask them to come if there were cases of breaches of discipline or similar things that would go against the orders. So each and every commander could see exactly from the observation point the deployment of their troops, if there was a need for any corrections. Otherwise, I inspected the area in order to provide expert assistance and exercise control, and then we dealt with issues on the spot, if there had been any issues to be dealt with. In other words, there was no need for them to come every day in order to avoid any waste of time or forcing the commanders to leave their command posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned breaches of discipline, and then you mentioned the inspection of fire in the air. The breaches of discipline, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I meant the deployment, the cases of bad camouflage, and if the order was not implemented to the full - and I'm talking about individual cases - in any case, one could observe the entire area from that place and the visibility was much better than if one were to go to the place where the combat was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When one mentions discipline, then we mean discipline in classical terms, but here you're referring to the PVO breaches of discipline?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about combat positions, camouflage, firing positions. If I can notice irregularities from the observation point, then everybody else can observe the same irregularities, and that's not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you have telephone communication with all the PVO positions or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. This was regulated by the order, and if there was fire or action we had to be able to communicate it directly with each other. Our aim was the most immediately one, our goal was the most immediate one and had to be implemented as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you say "aim" you mean the aircraft?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so, the enemy, the enemy aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please move into private session, Your Honours, because I would like to ask witness something that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You were in mid-sentence as far as the interpretation goes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Could we now see Exhibit 370, and then we will wrap up with this topic of resubordination. Thank you. If we can zoom in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, as it says here, this is an overview of composition of forces sent by the Chief of Staff of the 1st -- of the command of the 1st Military District, General Stojanovic, Vladimir Stojanovic, is sending this to the first administration of the armed forces of the SFRY on the 16th of November, 1991. You saw the first page of this document, of this report. What is it actually?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see in this cover letter, it seems that the first administration which was in charge of combat readiness asked for the command of the 1st Military District to send an overview, survey of their forces and technical equipment in units, and their involvement in the area of responsibility of the 1st Military District, what was under the command of the 1st Military District up to the 16th of November, 1991; that was the cut-off date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2, which has table number 1 on it. This is great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, in this overview can you find, please, LA PD on the 80th Brigade and can you tell us based on this table in whose composition is this 80th Brigade on the 16th of November?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the OG South column, which is the third one, the first one is the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade. And then the next one is the 20th Brigade of the 46 Partizan Division, and then the next column is the 80th Motorised Brigade, where you can see exactly the units which were within it. You have the 1st Motorised Battalion, the 1st Engineering Battalion, LAP Artillery Battalion of the PVO, the Logistics Battalion, and the 1st Mixed Anti-armour Artillery Battalion. So these are all of the units which comprised the 80th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at the Guards Motorised Brigade within OG South, do we see within its strength the units that were resubordinated to it but did not represent its regular strength?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Those units that resubordinated are shown in this table, so we see a Howitzer artillery battalion 155 from the Guards Mechanised Artillery Regiment. And then we see Howitzer artillery battalion from the 80th Motorised Brigade. It was Artillery Battalion 105, so it was resubordinated. And you don't see it underneath. Rather, in this overview you can see it in the unit to which it was resubordinated; this was a temporary measure, this was a temporary step. And as long as the resubordination was in force, this unit was in the organisational structure and carried out all of the orders which were issued to it by the commander of the unit to which it was resubordinated. That is to say, they had no links to their original unit on whose strength they were prior to resubordination. After the resubordination expires, a document is issued ordering this unit to return to its original unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you something else about what you said earlier. When a unit is resubordinated to another unit outside of its original composition, who does it send -- report to during the period of resubordination, to its original unit or to the unit it is resubordinated to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: For the purposes of resubordinated unit, its original unit does not exist any longer. It may have some formal links with it, just, you know, to have continuity, but all its duties now are addressed to that unit that is resubordinated and it is only to that unit that it sends reports, solely to them, once it is resubordinated. Once the resubordination expires, then they go back and are placed under the command of its original unit. There cannot be dual system. They cannot be responsible to both units, the original one and the one to which they were resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not be needing this document any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We could now turn to a topic which has to do with your work in the command of OG South. Tell me, please, did you go to the command of OG South; and if so, what tasks did you have there, what assignments?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I went regularly to attend daily briefings at the headquarters of OG South. This was under the command of the commander of OG South, General Mrksic. Those were regular visits, and naturally there were interim visits as well, as needed. If there was an urgent need, then we would go without waiting for a daily briefing. In addition to myself, there were other commanders there, commanders of subordinated units and the command of the brigade as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In addition to being present at daily briefings, did you have any other duties at the command of OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as I arrived in the area, in the area of Negoslavci and Vukovar, among other duties the command must also establish duty shifts and duty work. First it was at the level of the Guards Brigade, and later on at the level of OG South. And naturally, based on a list, I would occasionally have to be on duty; just like all other organs, there was a rota, and it was drafted by the operations organ of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us now examine these two tasks, these two duties. First of all, when it comes to duty work at the command of OG South, please tell me, when did you assume your duty post and how long would shifts start?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, shifts would normally start at 1800 hours. At 1700 hours we would have the briefings, and following them a duty shift would start and would last until morning hours, until 7.30 a.m. or until 10.00 a.m. on the following day. There was an instruction on the duty service. Perhaps you are wondering why this was not done in the morning hours, why there was no duty post in the morning, because the operations organ was normally present there in the morning hours so there was no need to put anyone else on duty because this other person was probably needed elsewhere. And it was mostly chiefs of various branches that were tasked with being on duty. This kind of organisation was very successful, very efficient. At the time, duties and obligations were articulated. We knew what was going on. We would normally be told whether there were any changes in the organisation structure, whether any new forces had arrived, had been deployed to the area. So people on duty shifts had to be briefed on everything so that they could have most up-to-date information and they could enter the relevant information into working maps and other documents. Naturally, there was also a log-book of the duty officer, and that book was there to record all of the observations about anything that might have taken place and had to do with the functioning of OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said all of the events having to do with OG South. You meant during the duty hours, duty shift?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, starting at 1800 hours when we assumed this duty post, until we were relieved by another person. So anything that might have taken place, any events, upon being assessed to see whether there was anything urgent, if the duty officer was unable to make a decision on his own or the matter was very important, then they would wake up the commander who was there in the vicinity. They would consult the commander, inform him of what had happened if there was a need to decide on something overnight. The post of the duty officer was located at the command post; that was a secure location, it was secured so that access was restricted. Only authorised persons were allowed to enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you say that only authorised persons were allowed in, do you mean that officers not belonging to a unit were not allowed entry?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was clearly defined who had access, who could gain entry.
