Officers who did not belong there and who might have had any problems had to resolve those problems through their own superiors, because the command of OG South, the headquarters of OG South, was not like a railway station where anybody who wanted to come whenever they wanted. That would undermine the subordination structure; that would make our work much more difficult, and it was against the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: However, if an officer -- a commanding officer from a superior command came to the duty post, such as from the 1st Military District, did they have to announce their arrival or could they just come in?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: There was security detail in front of the duty office, and they had to announce their arrival because the security officer did not have to necessarily know all of the superior officers. And if somebody came there with a proper business, then they had to inform of what it was and then they would gain entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But even that officer who was there on a relevant matter could not come in without informing the security officer?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. They -- unless they came in by force, but they couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You spoke earlier about how a duty officer had to decide when to wake up the commander. What would happen if the duty officer decided not to wake up the commander? How would he resolve anything that might arise?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, only if it was within his scope of authority he would decide to take certain measures, but when it came to other issues then he would have to make a judgement call as to whether wake up the commander or not. And that better be relevant because one couldn't just go in and wake up the commander, and this is why only responsible officers were placed there because they were trusted with that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now that you mentioned this waking of commander, please tell us based on your experience, when did Colonel Mrksic normally go to sleep, how long did he stay working?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: He worked long hours, slept very briefly, at least based on what I know. Whenever I was on duty, he would normally go to bed at midnight, 1.00 a.m., and he would get up early in the morning. He would be the first one to rise. Duty officers had to inform him of anything that might have happened, that was relevant and might have happened overnight. All matters that pertained to all of the organisational units within OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If anything that happens during a shift of duty is reported by the duty officer and duly entered in his records, what about information received by other members of the command during a shift of duty, that entered in the same book or is this information first shared with the duty officer, who then enters the information into the book?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I entirely understand your question, but I will give an answer anyway. All the information that is received is received through the duty officer. We're not the centre of the world, aren't we? Everything goes through the duty officer for that precise reason, so that all information is channeled into a single place. And then if another organ has to take measures that they're authorised to take, well then that very much depends on the situation, on the deadlines, and what have you. Without waiting for the commander to wake, if it's something to do with organisation, with the work of the organ and order him -- but rather, he knows immediately and the very next day he'll get an order and take official measures. Given the fact that the Guards Brigade was a very good team so there was never any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And what about orders received during the night, during a shift of duty. For example, an order from the 1st Military District or any superior command.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: We received both orders and information from the General Staff, from the federal secretariat, what should have gone, let me say, across because of greater efficiency and in order for whatever it was to get there as soon as possible. So a duty officer should have studied the document, not really sleep on it but study the document quickly, see what his superiors were on about, and take appropriate measures. If there was sufficient time, the duty officer will have no need to wake the commander at all, rather he would wait until the following morning. If not, well then he would have to wake the commander and this would have to be dealt with immediately. Speaking of information, information will be gone through. It was all recorded right there. The subordinate organs were called assistant commander for moral guidance at the time, based on this information produced our own information summaries which were signed by the commander, and those were then submitted to lower-level unit commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, when a duty officer receives an order from a superior command, he must make a judgement then how urgent it was and then decide whether to wake the commander or wake him the next morning. Is this a criterion that he uses while deciding whether he should wake the commander or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: He's sufficiently trained as a rule to be able to judge for himself and see what he has to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Speaking of orders, you say you attended those regular briefings. At those briefings, did the commander issue any orders? Where were these orders recorded if so? Was there some sort of a briefing record being kept?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, there was a briefing book, just like a duty officer kept a log where he had to record everything, everything that was going on, any orders received, any information, that sort of thing. Much along the same lines, at briefings there was a book in which everything was recorded that went on during a briefing and a briefing was always chaired by an operative officer. In the brigade this was Trifunovic or in his absence another person was appointed to chair these meetings. Any observations were recorded made by subordinate officers, their requests were recorded as well as anything that the commander had ordered. What is typical of most of these briefings is Colonel Mrksic, or General Mrksic, would give orders and draw everybody's attention to the issue of behaviour, attitude, and treatment of those taken or captured or wounded. He spoke a lot about the need to protect people. In one word, he drew everybody's attention to the need to watch our behaviour because we had all sorts of units in that area and there was certain units that had never before been part of our own composition. We did -- had next to no time and no insight into how those units were organised in some cases. For that reason and because of the peculiar nature of the task that we had to carry out, he would draw everybody's attention to the fact that our best behaviour was needed and that we needed to strictly abide by the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What you just said, I'm going to show you two exhibits to see what you know about them. Exhibit 415 first, please. Thank you very much. If we could just blow it up slightly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This is an order of the command of the 1st Military District dated the 18th of November, 1991, received by OG South on the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we received an initial notice of what this witness was going to testify to, and we received a second notice of what this witness is going to testify to. And we received proofing notes at approximately quarter of 11.00 last night, which we appreciate very much. But it appears that we're outside of the notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything about that; we don't receive them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The -- and also for the record, while I'm up here, we've received two initial proofing notes pursuant to 65 ter, and I'm very -- I'm sorry, two summaries. And half or more of what we've received and what's going to be testified to today is beyond anything that we've received. And I just want to make a note of this for the record. We're getting to that issue of quasi alibi or we might be into the issue of quasi alibi again. We might -- there's references to Kocic -- Koric and the departure of Mr. Kocic and Mr. Mrksic by vehicle for Belgrade. And this -- these notes obviously were not available when Mr. Koric testified so we could not put any of this to Mr. Koric. And we're just, based on the notes of last night, far beyond anything that was ever mentioned previously. And it might cause a need for cross-examination tomorrow as opposed to today, but we'll see how things go. We might have to make that request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. The Chamber has stressed before to counsel the requirement of the Rule that the information provided is required to indicate the nature of the evidence that will be given. And we've had quite a constant problem with inadequate summaries of the facts to which the witness will depose. At the moment, Mr. Vasic, Mr. Weiner does no more than place this on record, but we would simply underline the need for these summaries to be better than they are even know. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, can we just look at this order, please, that arrived on the 19th of November. Do you remember -- we'll look at the substance - was this order the subject of an order later issued by the commander of OG South or was this order the subject of regular briefings?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please just scroll down the page a little where it says "order" so that we know what we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Item 1 details the tasks of OG South for that morning, 10.00 to be more specific on the 19th of November, 1991. In cooperation with TG North, Tactical Group North, take the hospital and clear the remaining parts of town of any Ustasha forces, but I'm not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go to item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Item 3 of this order, Mr. Lesanovic. Can you please read what it was that the commander of the 1st Military District had ordered. Do you remember or know anything about what the OG South command did?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll read item 3 in its entirety. "Orders of the command of the 1st Military District. In carrying out the above orders, as in all other activities in the area of engagement of units of the 1st Military District, on crushing Ustasha forces, in all things comply with the Geneva Conventions on the prisoners of war." This came in on the 18th or the 19th. I'm not -- I didn't see the front. At previous briefings, the commander of the OG addressed the problem on a daily basis. We all had an aide-memoire, each of us. I actually have a copy on me, I can show it to you if you like, an aide-memoire showing us what steps to do or to take. The -- and as we said as a brigade command we prepared that and I have a copy of that and I can show you if you like on a single A4 sheet of paper all typed up. Copies were made to be submitted -- to be forwarded to all those involved so everybody knows what, when, where, how, all levels, how to treat a prisoner, how to treat a wounded prisoner. I don't want to repeat myself now. I have that aide-memoire. I have this other thing, I can show you that if you like, the other thing that was done for clashes during the aggression in 1999. The only thing being it was no longer the JNA, it was the Army of Yugoslavia. I'm talking about the front page, and this was a very important point. It was stressed that no one had the right to deviate from the regulations. Organs of the command of the operations group, when touring the units would talk to people to make sure that everybody was familiar with this, since to a large extent our forces were made up of reservists. So what was written here was no news to us. There had been orders before to this effect, and all these important things were also pointed out regularly to us at our regular briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with any orders by the commander of OG South to set up local commands, a town command; and if so, what was the reasoning behind this order?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The reasoning behind the order to set up local commands was to establish control over the area covered by OG South. The idea was to organise and set up command posts. In one word, once all these activities have been -- had been concluded, there were many things that needed doing and it was simpler to have this entire area subdivided into several areas through the commander's order. That made it easier for everyone to monitor the situation on the ground. For as long as combat was still ongoing, there was no need for this in the area because it was a single area. After the end, it was necessary to go back to normal life, work, and control in this territory. Who was coming, who was going, who was staying, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We're talking not about a command post; we are talking about local commands, local commanders were in charge. What sort of powers did these local commanders have over areas under their local command?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: A local commander exercises command in that particular area. He issues orders to organise any situation, organise accommodation, organise those coming in and those leaving, in one word: Life and work. This is a form of local authority virtually.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We know what this means in B/C/S, and I will consult the interpretation service during the break to see whether this corresponds to the terms used by OTP interpreters to make sure that we are using the same term for local or town command. Thank you. You told us partially about what happened during briefings. You told us about when briefings started, at what time roughly. Were those briefings held daily during combat operations and how were orders disseminated or if orders were issued at briefings, how were they disseminated to lower-level units within OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The briefings were almost daily, except on a few occasions, as far as I can remember, when during that period of time the situation was quite dynamic and would have been almost impossible under the circumstances to hold briefings. It maybe happened once or twice, and it just meant that briefings were rescheduled, delayed, otherwise we had regular briefings at regular scheduled hours. These daily briefings were attended by the organs of the command and subordinated forces. Commanders who were directly -- in direct contact with the commander of OG South. They would receive tasks from the commander during briefings, from the commander of OG South. And then they would go back to their own units and they would inform subordinated units about it. Naturally, based on the totality of orders, based on everything that arrived to the command of OG South from their superior commands, these orders would be processed and then adapted to the level of OG South. And then via the chain of command of OG South, they would be disseminated to subordinated units. Based on those orders, subordinated commands would produce their own orders, and this is how it reached the end level, those who were actually implementing those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, down to which level were their written orders disseminated and from which level on was it only oral orders?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: From OG South and down to artillery battalions inclusive, there were only written orders. And then from artillery battalions down, oral orders, based on which the command of artillery battalion had to produce its written order and they also had to record it in their official notebooks. So this is what was done at the level of a battery, say. But let me tell you, when it comes to specialists' issues, then commanders of batteries also had to produce in writing a document that wasn't really an official document but was still in writing and would reflect the tasks that they received from their superior artillery battalion, including the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just received from my colleague here this comment. In previous transcripts and in the order itself, in the exhibit pertaining to place commands or town command, the following terms were used: Village command or command of a village or command in a village, whereas in Vukovar the following terms were used: In-town commander or commander in town, whereas here during today's session the interprets used the term "local command" or "local commanders," and I just wanted to reiterate that this is one and the same term relating to the town command or local command or commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I don't know if this is an appropriate time for a second break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vasic, where are you in the course of your examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not very far from the end, Your Honour. I don't think it will take me more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'd like time to look over things; is that the point at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we will be able to proceed quicker if we are to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 20 minutes to 1.00, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, we may continue with your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It might even take less than I originally planned. Please tell me, were you present at the Guards Brigade when its commander -- no, I will reformulate my question. Do you know the former commander of the Guards Brigade, Colonel Velimir Coric?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do. I had occasion to meet him immediately upon my arrival in the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing him in the Vukovar sector; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of November. In the morning hours, that is to say the entire morning up until 1500 hours, I was with the investigation officials and with Mr. Stankovic, a pathologist who is currently serving as defence minister. We were involved in establishing the identity of a soldier, a conscript, and if I remember a lance-corporal, that is to say there were three corpses that we found. After that, I came to the deployment area of the artillery battalion, and immediately after that Colonel Coric arrived, probably on some business, and he also visited the commanders from the PVO artillery battalion. And I myself heard a lot of nice things about the former commander. We exchanged few brief sentences. I told him that I needed to go to report -- or rather, to the briefing, which was scheduled for 1700 hours, to which he replied that he was aware of that because he had been at the command post and he wanted to use the time available to go and visit people that he knew with whom he had used to work and that he wanted to wait for us to complete our briefing. And then once the briefing was over, commander and he would go --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear where to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to the briefing and after the briefing was over, I was at the command post for a brief period of time and I went back to the area of deployment of the artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. The interpreters didn't hear a portion of your answer, but I will ask you again now. You said that after the briefing he was supposed to go to commander someplace, which commander and where?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Coric said: I know that you have your briefing and while you are busy with your briefing I will go and visit my PVO people, that's what he said. Then I will go back to Negoslavci and Colonel Mrksic is supposed to go to Belgrade with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned twice in your answer deployment area or deployment sector. Where was it and where did you see Colonel Coric?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I was at the observation post, and he came there. Commander of artillery battalion was there, Mijatovic, and then some other officers. I can't remember their names, but he knew all of them because he used to be their commander. And now that he already was there and he had some time available, he wanted to go see them and talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you said the observation post, is it at the winery, the one that you marked?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, that marked with number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said on the 20th of November you went to the briefing. Was Mr. Trifunovic present as well as Mr. Gluscevic, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all commanding officers were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, do you know whether on that day a map was drawn of combat operations at the headquarters of OG South, was it done there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't sound familiar to me, and in view of the date I don't see any need for that. Why would anybody be drawing a map on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: For example, in order to take it to the meeting with the defence secretary on the 21st, would that be plausible?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was an organ of the command and I knew the reason for Mr. Mrksic's trip, I see no logic in taking a map with him because he wasn't going there to report on anything. Why would he be taking a map with him? What kind of a map? The purpose of his trip was entirely difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This is nothing more than speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It is. There's no matter of direct knowledge here, Mr. Vasic, it's just a -- an attempt to reason, speculation in other words. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, on the 20th of November did you see anybody at the headquarters of OG South drawing a map of any sort?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Since you told us that you were at the headquarters, can you tell us who at the Negoslavci headquarters of OG South was in charge of drafting maps or drawing maps, who was typically doing that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as a rule this was a duty of the operations officer. But there was also another aspect to it, an esthetic one. And as a rule, the then chief of signals corps, Lieutenant colonel Jovan Petrovic, would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, another question for you. When you were at the headquarters in Negoslavci, did you ever see there the officers of the security administration, did you ever see them there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I can't remember whether I did and if so when. It would not have been a relevant thing for me because it had nothing to do with my work. Perhaps they were there; I just don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If the Chief of Staff signed an order instead of the commander, what would that mean in terms of military roles?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: That would simply mean that the commander was absent, that he wasn't there, and it was only under those circumstances when the person in charge, person number one, was absent that his deputy would sign some documents because he is the authorised deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lesanovic, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Now, Mr. Borovic, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one, Your Honour, I hope that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lesanovic, I am Novak Lukic. I represent Veselin Sljivancanin. On page 60 you answered a question put to you by my learned friend Vasic, and I would like to follow up on that question. He asked you about the 20th of November and about the headquarters in Negoslavci, whether Gluscevic and Trifunovic were there. Your answer was that all the command answers were there, they were there for this briefing. I would like to ask you this: You know that on the 20th of November the hospital was evacuated. Are you sure that Sljivancanin was at that briefing on that day, are you absolutely positive? You said that all the commanding officers were there; are you positive that he was there as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I answered. The question did not imply Sljivancanin, and now you're asking about Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you remember that on the 20th November in the afternoon my client attended the briefing in question.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be sure of whether Sljivancanin was there or not. I know about the others. I know that Gluscevic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that a certain number of issues were raised and that those were relative to the organisation of the troops for return and the war plan and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And one more question, please. Before this Trial Chamber we've had a number of witnesses who said that Sljivancanin very often toured the ground, and that's why he was very often absent from these briefings. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Phillip Weiner, I work with the Office of the Prosecutor and I'm going to be asking you some questions this afternoon. All right. Now, sir, two witnesses have testified in this case that the LAD PVO of the 80th was subordinated to you and the OG South. You disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I am unable to agree because that was not the case. Had it been subordinated, this probably would have been reflected in some document. Whatever was supposed to be resubordinated was resubordinated by an order of Operations Group South; it did not carry out any of its missions along a special axis, a separate axis. It carried out its assignments within the area of responsibility of its own brigade, under which it was throughout in terms of organisation. It never left its original composition simply because it wasn't necessary, except for the period of time when it was used for logistics. But that wasn't resubordination. It had to get its supplies from somewhere. That's my answer. It was never for a moment resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you know Colonel Milorad Vujanovic -- Vojnovic, the commander of the 80th Brigade, you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you're familiar with the 80th Motorised Brigade, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know that it had its command in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know that Colonel Vujanovic or Vojnovic attended the meetings at the OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: He was there, as he well had to be. He was the commander. He had to report on what he had done and he was due to receive further assignments for the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he was the commander -- being the commander of the 80th meant that -- strike that. And you know that the 80th was part of the OG South, the Operational Group South. So he had to be there to receive his orders.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he did in fact receive orders from Colonel Mrksic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: From Colonel Mrksic alone because he was subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So basically your testimony is, at its best, the 80th was subordinated to Colonel Mrksic in OG South and the anti-aircraft defence of the 80th was part of the -- the anti-aircraft defence was part of the 80th, so it was part of OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing wrong with that, but that's no way to look at it. We can't assume that there was some sort of a double resubordination. I'm not sure what the reasoning is or the intention behind what you are suggesting. The 80th Brigade was a component of OG South, subordinated to the commander for this mission. But we can't take it out of his composition and then put it somewhere and then have some sort of double resubordination, which is just not the case. The artillery battalion command was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's look. Let's take it step by step. You said that you wanted to look at documents earlier or there were no documents. Let's look at some documents. Were you aware that the 80th Motorised Brigade maintained a war diary, are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: All units were required to keep war diaries, operations logs, as a document that remains for the posterity, and the same thing applied to the 80th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And being a war diary which covers November of 1991, all of those notes were placed in the diary in November of 1991, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: They should.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And they were placed in that diary in November at a time when the information was fresh or current?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: This was recorded -- or rather, all the activities happening during a particular day were recorded right there and then. It wasn't like they would let a day or two go by and then record something. All the information had to be authentic and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So all the information had to be authentic and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's look at the diary, which is Exhibit 375. May the witness please be shown that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please turn it around and zoom in a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you look at page 2 first. The date, November 9th at 2000 hours, which is 8.00 p.m., can you see that? The third paragraph where it refers to the PVO.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you read that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: "LAD PVO, acting according to plan" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Slowly, slowly, please, because they have to translate that into English. Sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Three or four words at a time. Okay. Could you read it, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: "LAD PVO acting according to plan and war assignments of OG South deployed as follows: First battery of LAD PVO at position in Grabovo sector. Second battery at position in Bokovci sector. The third with 30/2 in Vucedol sector. Second battery" -- my apologies. "Acted in the direction of Mala Dubrava sector, one military conscript wounded. A wound to the spine," I suppose, "who was sent to the Negoslavci hospital."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's sufficient. You don't have to mention his name in public. Now, sir, you agree that those three locations, Grabovo, Bokovci, and Vucedol were the three sectors where the anti-aircraft artillery were in fact located, that that is correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the deployment area for this artillery battery. They had received an assignment, and it was in keeping with these assignments and pursuant to that order -- but again I'm saying in relation to PVO. They were carrying out these assignments. If you look at this war log you can see that this is an organisational unit of the 80th Brigade because it was based on this that all activities were recorded in relation to all the other units of the 80th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move on. That was November 10th, we were hoping to start at the 9th, but that was the 10th --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies to my learned friend for interrupting, but I think it would be fair, if anything, to allow the witness to complete his answer. I think he was about to continue when my learned friend moved on to a different date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That was -- I had a specific question. He went beyond any question that I asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Re-examination later, if you wish, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let us move to November 12th, page 5 in the English, at 1700 hours, the second paragraph of 1700 hours. And it says: "LAD PVO is still at the same positions 1/LAD in Grabovo sector 2/LAD in Bokovci sector and 3/LAD in Vucedol sector and they continue to proceed in line with the OG South combat tasks." First, are those the proper locations? Is that correct? Are those the proper sectors where the anti-aircraft defences were located?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I apologise, but I must correct you. Not within the framework of OG South but rather within the framework of their own brigade because this is a war log of the 80th Brigade. It's not the war log of OG South --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me, sir. The question was: Are those the correct sections? It can be yes; it can be no. You have your own opinion. We're reading in the log of the 80th, and I'm asking you specifically about the language therein. The question: Are those the correct sectors that the anti-aircraft defences were located?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: But the previous sentence was: As part of OG South, but it wasn't within the framework of OG South. So I must correct you there. The sectors are correct because there was no need to change these positions, so they just kept their old positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And after the old positions it says: "And they continue to proceed in line with OG South combat tasks." Doesn't it say that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: In line with the assignments they received in the order because nothing else had changed. On that day they did not receive any additional assignments to fire at any targets on the ground from their commander. So this is all the activity that went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's look to the next page, which is the 13th of November. It's the first or the second after 5.30. Do you have it in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I don't. I have the 14th, the 14th and the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could he please be shown the 13th. It's on page 6 on the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you see the first, second, third, fourth, the fifth paragraph down -- arrest actually it would be the third paragraph down. Okay. Do you it, sir? I'll read it. "LAD PVO is still at the same positions. First LAD in Grabovo sector, second LAD in Bokovci sector and the third LAD in the Vucedol sector. It is under the OG South command." Is that what it says there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says but it's simply not accurate. There is no document to show that the artillery battalion was under the command of OG South; that's a contradiction. If this was under the command of OG South, what is it doing in this report, then it would be in the one of OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, when we started speaking about the war diary, you agreed that it was completed on a timely basis and the information had to be accurate and you agree that that is what it says there, it is under the OG South command. That's what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I never said the artillery battalion was under the command of OG South. When unifying tasks in terms of PVO, yes, but when resubordination was concerned, no, never. They received information on aircraft. They would exteriorise action and they would unify PVO activity, but not as far as targets on the ground were concerned. That was for their commander, but then this same artillery battalion got an assignment from the brigade commander and they had to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that the war diary is written for posterity. Those were your -- that was your statement. And you agree that it says here that the LAD PVO is under OG South command, and this is the war diary of the 80th Brigade talking about one of their units or units which has been resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, please have a look for yourself. The 3rd Motorised Brigade, it says above there, according to assignments of OG South. This is the way it was recorded -- it was the other way around --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lesanovic, you must slow down. You're speaking at a speed that is impossible for the transcript and the interpreters to keep up with. Now, just calm down and then try and answer at a more steady pace. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I'll try to slow down. If we look at the 13th and the other units -- well, then, for example up here you can see the 3rd Motorised Battalion, it's superfluous to go through and see what assignments it was carrying out on the day. It reads on the last line, if you look at that: "According to war assignments of OG South." Well, there -- here's a unit that's under the level of an artillery battalion, a Howitzer battalion, again it says: "Pursuant to orders of OG South." Well, probably if we looked at everything else there would be for the others, too, which means that a pattern was used to create this, whereas the duty was to previously look through it and check whether everything was right command --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you're just speculating about a pattern. What we do know here is this document says it is under OG South command. Doesn't it say that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: They are under the command of their 80th Brigade, end of story. No need to say anymore. What speculations are these? You can't have a single unit, be it part of OG South --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you agree that the document says it is under OG South command. You agree it says that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says, but that's simply not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not the commander of OG South that exercises command over the subordinate units of the 80th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'll get to that a little bit later, sir. Let's move to the next date, which is the 14th of November, the next page in the English. The only time is 1800 hours, and in English it's the seventh paragraph down. And you can see LAD PVO. And it says: "The LAD PVO is still at the same positions. It is proceeding in line with the OG South plan and combat tasks." Doesn't it say that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, since you do not have any documents stating that the LAD PVO was not subordinated to OG South and we have a document here, the war diary, which says it was in fact subordinated, would you now reconsider your testimony and state that it is very possible that it was subordinated to the OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I really do apologise. Please don't try to put words into my mouth. I can't change something that simply wasn't the case. As for those units that were resubordinated, there are specific documents indicating that there was resubordination. There are orders and decisions, and these are valid documents. This is just a record that might be accurate or inaccurate. It's pure statistics. It's about control, it's about skill, and it's about the level of training of units and commands to, in a concise way, and for each day draw up records and, in keeping with any orders received, get their units involved. There is not a single document that could be used to confirm that the PVO artillery battalion of the 80th Motorised Brigade ever, throughout its time in the area, was in fact resubordinated to the operations group. What that would mean is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But that document, sir, which is written by the brigade that brought the battalion there, that brought the battalion to Vukovar, indicated that that battalion was part of the OG South. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, everybody was part of OG South, but it did not have a direct line open to OG South and that's precisely what resubordination means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. If it's present, then what does resubordination mean? Say, provisional action taken for one unit in order to carry out a mission, have it resubordinated to another unit, be part of its composition, upon completion of a task it returns. That was definitely not the case with the PVO artillery battalion. As for this war diary, well they can write whatever they like. This is absolutely baseless because there isn't a single order that would provide a basis for what they reported here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you just said though before we started that war diaries have to be authentic and accurate, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's how they should be, but they are not a command document. They are nothing to base decisions on. This is a matter of pure statistics, what I'm telling you now. This is just writing down what happened. It may as well be erroneous if you give this sort of work to someone who's not sufficiently trained and doesn't know what to write. Let's allow for the possibility that errors occurred because the whole brigade consisted of reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you're just speculating because you don't even know who wrote that information in the war diary, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, don't you be telling me that I don't know. I was in the area and I suppose I know more than you. I can hardly have you tell me that sort of thing, that I don't know. If I don't know, I can't and please don't ask me --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: -- to confirm something that just isn't true. Am I supposed to repeat this a thousand times for your benefit, sir? An artillery battalion --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: -- of the 80th Brigade never at any time --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the question is, and I'll read it again: You're just speculating because you don't even know who wrote the information in that war diary, do you? And the question is: Do you know the name of the person who placed that information in that diary?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, allow me to remind you, it has been 15 years. Those were reserve officers and it would be simply ridiculous for me to know exactly who the operations officer was at the time in the 80th Brigade. Information should be entered by the operations organ or whoever is appointed by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue on in another area, and they are related these areas. You testified that you were chief of the anti-aircraft defence. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what were the dates that you were chief while in Vukovar, if you recall, sir? I know it's been 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand what date you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was the dates of your tenure that you served as chief of the anti-aircraft defence in Vukovar, so I assume sometime in -- at the beginning of October till what date?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. You mean from the time I arrived and all the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: From the 30th of September to the 24th of November, the return to the Belgrade garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during that time you established or the, the Operations Group South established, a unified anti-aircraft defence system. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it involved various units, not just guards motorised brigade units?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. As I said previously, I told you who was involved, all the units in the area, including the 80th Brigade artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you had control over that unified anti-aircraft defence system?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: By all means, but as far as the more specialised aspects were concerned, not in the command sense. I was not the commander. I was the chief of that particular branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you controlled the activities of the anti-aircraft units?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Which other one then?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me -- of the various units that made up that --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that -- now, during that time you testified that you were aware that the 80th moved from Grabovo to Ovcara on the 18th and 19th of November, say on or about the 18th of November in 1991. You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: That the 80th Brigade in its entirety moved; is that your question? I'm afraid I didn't understand. I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The LAD PVO of the 80th moved from Grabovo to Ovcara on or about the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: But not the artillery battery. This was only in reference to the command post --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The artillery battalion, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you authorise this move?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what we were talking about today, weren't we? There was no reason not to authorise it because the system had not suffered any disruptions and the order of its brigade commander had been carried out. This was moved based on an order of the commander of the 80th Brigade and not on any of my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, isn't it true that this move occurred on the basis of an order of Operational Group South?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The command of Operations Group South, there is no written document, there is no need, it did not order for the artillery battalion's command post to be moved, rather, the commander of the 80th Brigade as one of his decisions and ideas furthermore planned and carried out this decision, his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the commander of the Operational Group South could not have issued this order if the unit was not subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: By all means. The unit was not subordinated to him and he could not have issued and there would have been no need for him to have issued to him two units that weren't on a direct line. The commander of OG South had the brigade command on a direct line, but it doesn't exist -- I mean, no documents exist to show that orders were given to the -- that the order given by the commander of the 80th Brigade was and to move the position of the artillery battalion. The system had not suffered any disruptions because this was in his area of responsibility and there was no need to dispute this. And I assume that this was preceded by the next assignment that was given to him, appointing him local commander. First his command post was moved and then an assignment was given to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, isn't it true that Colonel Mrksic issued the order to move this unit to Ovcara, since this unit was subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The PVO artillery battalion was not subordinated to Mrksic. The PVO artillery battalion was subordinated to the commander of the artillery battery and to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you that the Operational Group South did in fact issue the order, moving this unit to Ovcara? Would that surprise you, sir, because wouldn't that indicate that this unit was in fact subordinated to Operational Group South?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: There is no such order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown Exhibit 401, which is the war diary of Operational Group South and the Guards Motorised Brigade. Could we go to page 39 in the English, which is November 18th, 0700 hours, 7.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could we have also the page in B/C/S, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I don't have it, sir, page -- one moment. It's page 39 in the English. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you see November 18th? It's about four pages from the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The B/C/S reference for the benefit of my learned friend is 02935478.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, there are three --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I think we need the lower half of the page probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you see it says on the left: "Negoslavci village," and I'll read it to you. "Regulating the issue of closing down the axes and securing the area of," it looks like "Djakubovac [phoen], Ovcara, and Bokovci in connection with pulling the 20th Partizan Brigade out of combat deployment," and then the next word. "Order. 1. The LAD PVO 80th mtbr," which is motorised brigade, "is to be moved from the Grabovo sector to Ovcara." And if you look to the right there's a -- it says: "Signed Major Trifunovic." Is that what it says there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says. This is a result from a previous briefing and a proposal of the commander of the 80th Brigade that was carried out and converted into an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, does it say that this is a proposal of the commander of the 80th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so because this is an order. This is the command of operations group giving an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it's the command of the operations group giving an order that the LAD PVO 80th Motorised Brigade or of the 80th Motorised Brigade is to be moved from the Grabovo sector to Ovcara. Isn't that correct? That's where the order comes from on the 18th, Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: If we try to look at the paragraph just above, that's what precedes this assignment, commander of OG South calls brigade commander. He didn't call the artillery battalion commander to hand his assignments out to him. Isn't that what it says? And let's try not to repeat everything else. All the other units that are relevant for the fruition of this assignment. What do you think a brigade commander is? A courier for an artillery battalion commander. Does it say: "Commander of the artillery brigade"? No, it says commander of the 80th Brigade. So he's the one who received this assignment and the PVO artillery battalion is his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, it doesn't say the LAD PVO unit is his own. It doesn't say that this is being sent to the commander of the 80th Brigade, but it does say that it is ordered -- that there's an order or it's ordered that that anti-aircraft unit be moved from Grabovo to Ovcara, and that order is coming from Operations Group South. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I must correct you. It's not the unit. It's at the proposal of the commander of the 80th the command post is moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: The command post of the artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, does it say that at the request of the commander of the 80th Brigade or based on recommendations of that commander? It doesn't say any of that, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Excellent. Let's start with the assumption that this is indeed the case. The commander of OG South called --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, we're not --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: -- those responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: -- looking for speculation. You want to start -- we're not looking for speculation --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: We're not going to do that. I'm just going to try to explain. Please. This is an insult when you say "speculation." I find that insulting. Allow me to explain or stop insulting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: You -- you speculate about the way in which these units were involved; you are the one speculating. You're asking me to say something that is totally baseless. This is not a document; these are just notes. This is a recording. An official document is something that is written down when something is ordered. If you can read this, what it says is the commander called those responsible, whose presence was needed, he listened to them, what do you need, what would you like, and then that's what he did, through his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, this is signed by Major Trifunovic. Was he the operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. Now, sir, when did you first speak with the Defence counsel in relation to this case?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. This was last year sometime when I was still with the defence ministry. We agreed about some circumstances, whether I would like to testify about some issues. That was the first time I met Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you speak to him about this case?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. We weren't able to. We had no time for that. It was a brief exchange of information -- or rather, getting to know each other, first and foremost, and a more global kind of conversation, but nothing very individual because that would have required a lot of time and certainly it would have required me to jog my memory about a number of things 15 years later. So the answer is: Not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, today you spoke of a certain individual being named town commander. Now, in this case the Defence has filed on three occasions information from you or information concerning about what you're going to testify to. And on September 6th, 2006, they stated the follow as a summary of your testimony. "The witness will also testify that he was not informed that the OTP witness P014 was assigned by his commander Vojnovic to the position of the commander of Ovcara in the evening hours of 19 November 1991." Did you previously advise counsel that you were not aware that that individual was named as town commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: A strange and very confused question. Can you please repeat that. I don't understand. Can you ask me a specific one? I don't know what it is you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Today you testified that you were aware that a certain individual was named town commander. According to the Defence in their notes or their summary of your testimony a few weeks ago they indicate that you were not informed of this appointment. Did you previously tell the Defence that you were not aware that a certain individual was appointed as town commander of Ovcara? Did you tell them that? You're looking to the Defence. Could you look to us then? Did you ever tell anyone that you didn't know that? Was that something you just thought about yesterday when you spoke with counsel?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's not true because the commander of the 80th Brigade wrote an order, he wrote a document predicting and appointing who the local commander would be. That was no secret at all. I don't remember the specific name, but there's probably a document. You probably have it. There's a document -- an order by the commander of the 80th Brigade, among other things, appointing a local commander, P014. That is Ovcara. And I did say today, didn't I? He told me, he met me, the same day the commander gave that order appointing him as commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's time for the end of the session, and we can continue with this tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we leave, if my learned friend could just give me a reference for what he has been showing the witness, what he showed the witness a while ago, because I can't seem to be able to track that down and I need to track it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll give you a copy of that at the break. I'll give you my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing. I know we're past the mark already, but I do have one motion, Your Honour. It's about our exchange with the OTP and about the proposal in relation to our client's evidence. What -- we asked to be able to file a new reply to the Prosecutor's motion. We would like to do this orally. I even talked to Mr. Weiner and said that Mr. Moore and Ms. Riley [as interpreted] should come, too. Maybe they have further arguments. I think it would greatly speed up the proceedings if we could address this orally to challenge some points and leave others unchallenged. Tomorrow when we're done with this witness I suppose there will remain sufficient time to give out final arguments, both parties I mean, and then it's down to you, Your Honours. I think a lot has been clarified by the previous motions. There are things that have been agreed on and things we couldn't agree on, but there are still legal issues pending, so could we please have oral arguments about that tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, if that's convenient to both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That should be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If there is time. We adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 22nd day of

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
